texte.80cd9a5172a6: To bring the rook to the open c-file.

texte.c4ff6086aaa0: After {z1}, Black has moved a second kingside pawn with {z2} ({v1}). Which of the two moved pawns now stands without pawn protection, and which white piece is already attacking it? Which black pawn has lost a protector through {z3}? And which of the four reasons for a pawn move from Section 5.1 does {z4} fulfill?
texte.4ea56b9d0bca: The pawn on h6 stands without pawn protection: only a pawn on g7 could protect it, and the g-pawn is already on g6, from where it cannot go back. Only after {z1} would the h-pawn be protected by g6 again. Since {z2}, the diagonal c1–h6 has been open, and the bishop on c1 attacks h6. For now, the bishop on f8, the knight on g8, and the rook on h8 still defend it. The pawn that has lost a protector is g6: before, f7 and h7 protected it; now only f7 does. If the f-pawn moves, g6 stands without pawn protection. {z3} fulfills none of the four reasons: it does not gain an important square, does not create a weakness for the opponent, does not get an attack going, and does not open a path for any piece. Remember: a second pawn move on the same wing often doubles the price of the first.
texte.0995a240189c: The pawn on h6 no longer has pawn protection and is already in the sights of the bishop on c1; g6 has lost a protector, h7. 2... h6 fulfills none of the four reasons for a pawn move.
texte.8a4196215831: Apply the protection test to the black pawns in {v1}: Which pawns fail it, and which weakness from this chapter does each one have? Then count the pawn islands of both sides. Which side is structurally better according to the rule of thumb, and what does the other side have as compensation?
texte.eb7a795c292c: Two black pawns fail the protection test: the pawn on a7 is an isolani, since there is no black pawn left on the b-file. The pawn on c6 is backward: its neighbor d5 is already ahead of it, and there is no pawn on the b-file that could protect it. The pawn on d5, on the other hand, is healthy, because c6 protects it. The islands: Black has three (a7, c6–d5, and f7–h7), White only two (a2–c2 and f2–h2). According to the rule of thumb, White is therefore structurally better. In return, Black has the half-open b-file, on which a rook can put pressure on the pawn on b2, and active bishops. Remember: the protection test shows you which pawns will tie down pieces later.
texte.cb713a847f13: a7 is an isolani, c6 a backward pawn; Black has three pawn islands, White two. White is structurally better; in return, Black has the half-open b-file against b2 and active bishops.
texte.7d44ea6ee6df: Which of the two black bishops in {v1} is the “bad” one and which is the “good” one? Explain your answer. Which white bishop is bad by the same standard?
texte.d2bbf851a194: The bishop on f8, which travels on dark squares, is the bad bishop, since both d6 and e5 are dark squares and block its diagonals. The bishop on c8 is the good one, because the central black pawns do not stand on its light color: exactly the opposite of the French Advance Variation, where the light-squared bishop on c8 was the bad one. For White, d3 and e4 stand on light squares, so the light-squared bishop on f1 is the bad one. Remember: what decides is not the color of the bishop itself, but the color on which your own pawns stand.
texte.02810b8d6343: The black pawns d6 and e5 stand on dark squares, so the dark-squared bishop on f8 is the bad one and c8 the good one. For White, d3 and e4 stand on light squares, which is why the bishop on f1 is the bad one.
texte.8b1934de7908: Carry out the complete skeleton X-ray for the position in {v1}: answer all four guiding questions for White and for Black, and then formulate a plan in one sentence for each side. Compare the result with the French Advance Variation from Section 5.7: where does the most important difference lie?
texte.91f333e1311c: Squares: The e5-pawn takes d6 and f6 away from Black, and the d5-pawn takes c4 and e4 away from White. There is no hole that either side could use immediately. Pawns: White's base d4 fails the protection test, since the c-pawn has been traded and the e-pawn already stands ahead of it. That is why the knights on b3 and f3, the bishop on e3, and the queen on d1 guard it. For Black, everything is healthy: d5 is protected by e6, e6 by f7. Both sides have two pawn islands. Direction: White's chain points to the kingside, and White has space there. Black's chain points to the queenside. The lever {z1} has already been played, and Black is now pressing on d4 with pieces and using the open c-file. Pieces: The center is closed. Black's bishop on f5 stands outside the chain and is active. White's bishop on e3 stands on the color of its own chain, but is busy defending d4. The rooks of both sides belong on the open c-file. Plans: White: “I use my space on the kingside, fight for the open c-file, and secure my base d4 with pieces.” Black: “I use the open c-file and my active bishop on f5, attack the base d4, and secure my kingside.” The most important difference from the French Advance Variation lies in the fourth guiding question: Black has no locked-in bishop, because Black developed it before {z2}. Remember: the same pawn structure can turn out quite differently for the pieces. That is why the fourth question is always part of it.
texte.d2a98cc3907c: White's base d4 is weak and ties down pieces, and White has space on the kingside; Black presses against d4 via the open c-file. Unlike in the French Advance Variation, Black has no locked-in bishop, because Black developed it before ...e6.
texte.92f987669ecf: d5 is a permanent hole in Black's camp, supported by the e4-pawn – an ideal square for a knight. The knight on c3 already guards it.
texte.bd605a5be1de: The e5-pawn takes the squares d4 and f4 away from White. There is no white hole that Black could use permanently. d5 is watched by the bishop on e6, the knight on f6, and later the knight on d7 via b6.
texte.b172996e7b41: White wants to bring a knight to d5 and keep it there. Black overprotects d5 with pieces, wants to drive away the knight on c3 with {z1} and {z2}, and prepares the freeing move {z3}, which closes the hole. That is why White plays {z4}: the pawn prevents {z5}, and the knight on c3 remains the guard of d5.
texte.2715de29f2fc: e5, supported by the d4-pawn, is the springboard for a white knight.
texte.680322ab1abd: No white pawn can attack d5, in front of the isolani, anymore: the blockade square. Black already controls it with the bishop on b7, the knight on f6, and the pawn on e6.
texte.9ed169bd0cdc: d4 fails the protection test: no white pawn can ever protect it. Three pawn islands.
texte.693d59f0b6d5: Healthy: b6 is protected by a7, e6 by f7. Two pawn islands.
texte.38c44385fa2a: White needs piece activity now and avoids exchanges. Black blockades d5, trades pieces, and steers toward an endgame. Black starts with {z1}: one piece has been traded, and the isolani becomes the pair c3–d4. The pawn on d4 is now protected, but c3 fails the protection test and stands on the c-file, which is half-open for Black: the target moves from d4 to c3. Black holds the pair in place with pieces on c4 and d5. If c3 does advance to c4, they become hanging pawns.
texte.592fe3735944: The squares in front of the black pawns, b4, c4, d4, and e4, are still under their control. If one of them advances, a hole appears: after {z1} on d4, after {z2} on c4.
texte.9a77709a649f: The knight on f6 can jump to e4, supported by the pawn on d5.
texte.20cc4be8e369: Healthy: two pawn islands (a2–b2 and e3–h2).
texte.106946cd882a: Of c5 and d5, only one ever passes the protection test: if one advances, the other protects it and is then left behind without protection itself, because there is no black pawn left on the b- or the e-file. Three pawn islands (a7, c5–d5, and f7–h6).
texte.ecb8cbc4a90c: White puts the two pawns under pressure: the rook on c1 against c5 as soon as the knight on c3 clears the file, later a rook on the d-file against d5. Good first moves are {z1} or {z2}: both attack the knight on d7, which protects c5. Black keeps the pawns together and looks for active play with the pieces. Black moves one of the pawns only when it threatens something concrete.
texte.38534d1a51b6: The e5-pawn takes the squares d6 and f6 away from Black: the knight on g8 had to take the detour via h6 to f5.
texte.bd88719b1b35: The d5-pawn controls c4 and e4. The knight on f5 is safe as long as White does not play {z1}.
texte.998bb636aefb: The base d4 has lost its support c3 and fails the protection test.
texte.f97dfb4cf0b2: The base e6 is protected by the pawn on f7.
texte.79d83e9dfe71: The chain points to the kingside: White has space there.
texte.1d3b17e6aa50: The chain points to the queenside, and the c-file is open: that is where Black plays, against d4.
texte.bf300dae3ee2: Three black pieces attack d4, and only two white ones defend it. White must act immediately: after {z1}, {z2} wins a pawn. That is why Chapter 2 continues with {z3}: the knight attacks the queen, one of the three attackers, and thereby gains time.
texte.8a78e97f91ec: e5, supported by the d4-pawn, is a typical knight square as long as Black does not play {z1}.
texte.e7742f2ac3f5: e4, supported by the d5-pawn, is a typical knight square as long as White does not play {z1}.
texte.d1ac3ce0dbc9: Healthy before the minority attack; afterwards c6 is backward and a7 isolated ({v1}) – or d5 becomes an isolani.
texte.3f63cdc21768: Minority on the queenside (2 against 3): White plays there with {z1}.
texte.adc10faaff47: The majority on the queenside is blocked by the minority attack. Counterplay comes with pieces on the kingside, for example with {z1} and {z2}.
texte.236623383f48: With the minority attack, White creates a permanent target on the queenside and starts with {z1}, prepared so that {z2} can follow. Black must be faster on the other wing.
texte.23ec3a93959a: e5 is a good square for a white knight as soon as the knight on c6 and the queen on d6 no longer both cover it; of the black pawns, only the f-pawn (after {z1}) can still watch over it.
texte.4faa1ff82bf9: e4 is held by the bishop on d3 and the knight on d2. Neither side has a permanent hole.
texte.1000379d675b: Healthy: c3 and e3 protect d4, b2 protects c3, f2 protects e3.
texte.8fe70c208c09: Healthy: d5 is protected by e6, e6 by f7.
texte.468939a451a6: The lever {z1} attacks d5 and opens the center.
texte.546a7606e899: The lever {z1} attacks d4; alternatively {z2} with play on the queenside.
texte.523dfffac281: The bishop on d3 is good, because White's center pawns stand on dark squares. White wants to open the center so that the bishop and the rooks can work.
texte.c5d308f873d0: The bishop on d7 is bad: d5 and e6 stand on light squares. Only {z1} opens the diagonal d7–h3 for it.
texte.4ffcc067e025: Both sides want to open the center, but for different reasons: White, so that the good bishop and the rooks can work; Black, to free the bad bishop. White starts with {z1}: the rook prepares {z2}. Black can answer with a lever of its own, {z3}.
texte.ecd773900fc3: The e5-pawn takes d6 and f6 away from Black. White could drive away the strong knight on f5 with a pawn only by {z1}, and this move would weaken White's own king.
texte.1b278d04d7dd: The d5-pawn holds c4 and e4: white pieces cannot settle there permanently.
texte.deee07d967db: The base d4 fails the protection test. Two pawn islands.
texte.c19601ca79d9: Healthy: d5 is protected by e6, e6 by f7. Two pawn islands.
texte.0f22dcd2ed11: The chain points to the kingside, and White has space there. White wants to occupy the open c-file too.
texte.ae2b39b2ddce: The chain points to the queenside, and the c-file is open. The lever {z1} does attack the head of the chain, but it makes the f-file half-open for the rook on f8.
texte.72095c3f728e: The center is closed. The bishop on e2 is good, because d4 and e5 stand on dark squares. The knight on f3 and the queen on d2 have to guard d4.
texte.5ec3e5f1542a: The knights on c6 and f5 attack d4 and are active. The bishop on d7 is bad: d5 and e6 stand on light squares.
texte.ccd483f24d3f: White secures d4 with more pieces and uses the extra space. Black presses on d4, occupies the c-file, and with {z1} makes the f-file half-open for the rooks, after which the bishop on d7 also finds new paths.
texte.ad0e63060679: Holes in front of your own king
